news.title: With the biggest IPO of all time, Anthropic’s ‘good guy’ reputation is on the line
news.title_en: With the biggest IPO of all time, Anthropic’s ‘good guy’ reputation is on the line
news.author: Hayden Field
news.content_snippet:
Today is a new beginning for Anthropic: a years-in-the-making IPO that beat out SpaceX for most valuable of all time, having raised $81.3 billion and set an important precedent for the other public AI lab debuts to come. But it’s not simply a financial milestone.

Anthropic was founded on the idea that it prioritized safety more than other labs; its founders had left executive research positions at OpenAI. As the AI race has accelerated, though, its executives have emphasized that Anthropic can
news.summary_en: AI lab Anthropic has completed the largest-ever IPO in history, raising $81.3 billion. Operating as a Public Benefit Corporation, the company utilizes a unique Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT) structure to retain voting control, aiming to navigate the inherent tension between aggressive AI development and its foundational commitment to safety.
paragraphs: Today is a new beginning for Anthropic: a years-in-the-making IPO that beat out SpaceX for most valuable of all time, having raised $81.3 billion and set an important precedent for the other public AI lab debuts to come. But it’s not simply a financial milestone.

Anthropic was founded on the idea that it prioritized safety more than other labs; its founders had left executive research positions at OpenAI. As the AI race has accelerated, though, its executives have emphasized that Anthropic can only fulfill this mission by coming in first place, requiring lots of money and compute. Unsurprisingly, thoughtful, safe, and intentional AI development can conflict with the kind of sheer speed that winning this race requires. Adding in an initial public offering only complicates things further, and Anthropic’s leadership can pursue it more or less unilaterally. That’s thanks to a corporate structure focused on insulating the company from shareholder pressure to turn a profit — but one that also removes typical checks on its power.

One former Anthropic employee, who left ahead of the IPO, said he and others at Anthropic have increasingly been feeling that the current pace of AI development is “untenable under normal market structures,” particularly with the mismatched incentives at play in a powerful industry with little to no oversight.

Anthropic has spent years billing itself as different from, and more careful than, other AI companies. In theory, this extends to its plan for going public. It’s registered as a Public Benefit Corporation, which means Anthropic’s board has a responsibility to balance its mission against shareholder wealth maximization. As my colleague Robert Hart has discussed before, it has also developed a highly unusual power structure.

Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT), introduced in 2023, and its founders have controlling voting rights, meaning they’d never be able to be voted out by shareholders even as a public company. A special class of stock, Class T, allows a small group of trustees — the members of the LTBT — the “authority to select and remove a portion of” Anthropic’s board. They exist outside typical shareholder pressure and theoretically are a check for the founders, tasked with a mission to “balance the financial interests of our stockholders and our public benefit purpose at key junctures where we expect the consequences of our decisions to reach far beyond Anthropic.”

The reality is significantly more complicated. The LTBT technically chooses four members of Anthropic’s seven-person board, for instance, but one of those four effectively needs to be approved by Anthropic’s founders, leaving the trust short of straightforward majority control. There are also stipulations about nominating or removing a director: the LTBT must provide its decision with 30 days’ notice to the company’s “nominating and corporate governance committee,” which consists of three members: co-founder Daniela Amodei (who is chair of the committee), Netflix co-founder Reed Hastings, and Anthropic investor Yasmin Razavi.

Though the LTBT members are “financially disinterested” in the company, there’s also nothing stopping Anthropic from hypothetically hiring away a trustee and paying them a lot of money to work for the company. Mariano-Florentino Cuéllar (a former trustee) joined Anthropic in August as its Chief Global Affairs Officer, and OpenAI has in the past hired a former board member, Fidji Simo, to an executive position within the company. One could imagine a scenario in which, if a trustee was “looking a little bit too activist-y or something, they could just make that trustee an offer with millions of dollars in effective compensation that would entail stepping down from the trust, and that’s one way that they could have some oversight over this,” said Tyler Johnston, founder of The Midas Project, a nonprofit AI industry watchdog.

Although the LTBT is billed as a way to check Anthropic’s leadership, to some outside observers, the fine print looks shaky. “The trust, since it doesn’t have a financial interest in Anthropic, could theoretically use its power with three slash four directors to keep the company on mission,” says Ann Lipton, law professor at the University of Colorado Law School and an expert in corporate governance. “One might question how likely that is to occur.”

Moreover, Lipton questions whether the trust would know enough to gauge when to hit the brakes on a company plan or product even if they did have such authority. The four listed LTBT members aren’t known to be AI experts: they include former Fed Chair Ben Bernanke, foreign policy analyst Richard Fontaine, experimental physicist Christopher Stubbs, and former GiveWell executive Neil Buddy Shah, who is chair of the LTBT. “I’m not convinced that the trustees or the directors that they appoint have the insight into AI and AI development to be able to make these choices,” Lipton says. “They’re very prestigious people, but what does Ben Bernanke know about AI?”

Several experts compared Anthropic’s LTBT to OpenAI’s nonprofit board before Altman’s ouster: “The powers, or lack thereof, of the Long-Term Benefit Trust … [are] analogous in some ways to the powers that the OpenAI nonprofit has,” said The Midas Project’s Johnston. Of course, that board’s decision to oust OpenAI CEO Sam Altman ended up leading, days later, to Altman’s return as CEO and the majority of the board’s resignation and replacement.

But there’s a notable difference between that and the LTBT. Before OpenAI’s restructuring, its nonprofit board had the ability to step in and guide day-to-day decisions at the company when deemed necessary, and even after its restructuring, they retained that ability for safety and security matters, such as delaying or stopping a model release. Anthropic’s Form S-1 suggests that the LTBT, with its main duty being appointing (and potentially removing) certain board members, does not have either of those levels of authority.
Instead, Anthropic’s structure looks more like the kind of founder-centric setup that Silicon Valley favors — like Mark Zuckerberg with Meta, and Elon Musk with SpaceX.
Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment.

“Neither the Trust or the trustees have any decisionmaking authority … over day to day decisions,” said Hamza Chaudhry, who leads AI and national security at the Future of Life Institute. “So I do not have strong hopes for the LTBT being a key mechanism for governance after they go public.”

The former Anthropic employee said that Anthropic’s founders are essentially the only ones with any real decisionmaking power: “I would be surprised if you could find anyone who knows the founders, knows the Long-Term Benefit Trust, understands how decisions get made, and thinks the Long-Term Benefit Trust has any meaningful power,” he said. The employee added that the trustees were both “poorly equipped to provide meaningful oversight” to the founders and also selected on purpose to not rock the boat.

Anthropic as a public company will face more pressure than ever before to secure capital, whether via driving more revenue or fundraising. That means that, as has been a trend in the industry for years, it will likely be more difficult to justify expensive AI safety initiatives, and there will inevitably be more pressure to speed up product releases and commercialization. “This trust and the founders together are the ones who actually have governance power,” Lipton said. “So you either trust that they are going to balance the interests of society appropriately, or you don’t. Either way, the real constraint on whatever societal impulses they have is going to be the fact that Anthropic needs money.”

Anthropic has been open about the fact that it’s in extreme need of cold, hard cash, particularly to buy more compute and speed up its AI advancement. “Compute is the deepest business dilemma that the company faces,” Amodei said last Friday in a livestreamed conversation with JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon. “If you buy too much, of course you can financially overextend yourself. If you buy too little, then you can’t support inference for customers, and even more importantly … you can’t do the R&D.”

Anthropic’s website summarizes the company’s raison d’être as one thing: “AI research and products that put safety at the frontier.” But it’s also been clear that for that safety pledge to matter, Anthropic needs vast resources to remain a viable business. Like other labs, it’s been pursuing recursive self-improvement, a controversial and potentially dangerous industry milestone denoting AI systems that can autonomously improve and create advanced versions of themselves. “You can’t do safety from second place,” said Anthropic policy chief Sarah Heck in September.

This explanation hasn’t satisfied everyone, including some Anthropic employees. Anthropic’s head of safeguards research departed in February alleging that “the world is in peril”; one of its researchers, Jacob Coxon, made headlines in September for claiming that both Anthropic and OpenAI are “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives”; and that same month, an Anthropic safety researcher departed for a job at nonprofit third-party AI auditor METR, writing that “AI companies are on track to impose an unprecedented level of risk on society” and that “while Anthropic hasn’t had as severe an incident as the HuggingFace attack [by OpenAI agents], I think that’s partly a matter of luck.”

On Wednesday, a new statement from the Center for AI Safety, with prominent industry signatories from Hugging Face, Harvard University, and more, alleged that Anthropic is “not a safe AI company” and that it attempts to “amass power in the name of the greater good.” It stated, “Anthropic warns that recursively self-improving AI could concentrate power and escape human control, yet races to build it first. The company uses safety branding to court investors, employees, and the public—even as it has quietly weakened its safety pledges and lobbied for self-serving regulation.”

The former Anthropic employee said he felt he had initially “drunk the Kool-Aid” about Anthropic needing to come in first place in the AI race for a safe outcome but then grew disillusioned, realizing that the race to the top did not “warrant the cost imposed” — namely, that one company should not be able to “unilaterally” decide to pursue RSI. (Amodei has stated publicly that “left unchecked, [RSI] could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems, and so must be pursued very carefully, if at all.”)

“It’s pretty ridiculous that private companies are building a new form of intelligence on track to be more powerful and influential on the planet than humans and are doing that with less oversight, in many ways, than taco trucks currently have,” the former employee said.

Anthropic’s website states that “at the end of the day, the mission is what we’re all here for. It gives us a shared purpose and allows us to act swiftly together, rather than being pulled in multiple directions by competing goals. It engenders trust and collaboration, and is the final arbiter in our decisions.” The question is whether, and how, the interpretation of Anthropic’s mission may shift — once it’s facing more pressure than ever before to justify a fully diluted market cap of about $1.5 trillion.

news.summary_en: AI startup Anthropic has completed its Nasdaq IPO, raising $81.3 billion and surpassing SpaceX's record, with a fully diluted market cap of approximately $1.5 trillion. Despite revenue surging 1,200% year-over-year to $33.24 billion in the first nine months, net losses widened to $104 billion due to the revaluation of convertible notes and derivative liabilities.
paragraphs: Claude developer Anthropic has surpassed SpaceX's previous record IPO. While tech giants are pouring in billions, a key early investor is warning about the consequences of an unchecked AI race.

Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 per share, beating the original target range of $70 to $78. Overwhelming demand pushed the public benefit corporation and its seven co-founders to sell roughly 980 million Class A common shares, up from a planned 825 million.

The offering raised $81.3 billion, according to a CNBC report, overtaking the previous record set by Elon Musk's SpaceX, which raised $75 billion in June. Anthropic's fully diluted market cap stands at about $1.5 trillion, while its market value excluding stock options sits closer to $1 trillion, according to the Wall Street Journal.

Shares begin trading Thursday on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol "ANT."The underwriting syndicate, including Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, also received a 30-day option to purchase an additional 147 million shares. Each of the seven co-founders is selling 3.38 million shares for a combined $1.96 billion, none of which flows to Anthropic itself.
### Claude Code sends revenue soaring as losses climb into the billions

Founded in 2021 by former OpenAI researchers led by CEO Dario Amodei, Anthropic saw explosive growth in its enterprise business in 2026, fueled by the coding tool Claude Code. Revenue surged about 1,200 percent year over year to $33.24 billion in the first nine months through September 30. By the end of October, annualized revenue had already reached roughly $81 billion.

Net losses for the same nine-month period widened from $25.1 billion a year earlier to $104 billion, driven primarily by revaluations of convertible notes and derivative liabilities. Amazon and Google rank among the largest shareholders, each holding stakes worth more than $100 billion. Together with Microsoft, Nvidia, and AMD, these tech giants are investing another $26 billion at the offering price. They also sell Anthropic expensive hardware, counting the company as a customer.

The IPO amounts to a stress test for the AI industry, which has recently been rattled by rising interest rates for data center developers, political headwinds from the U.S. midterm elections, and the ousting of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang last week. Anthropic itself clashed with the U.S. government twice this year over safety issues and lists risk factors across more than 90 pages in its prospectus. Rival OpenAI, meanwhile, has confidentially filed for an IPO planned for 2027.
### Early investor Dustin Moskovitz warns of an unchecked AI race

Amodei said in a roadshow video that the technology could usher in an age of wonders with careful risk management, but one of Anthropic's most important early investors disagrees. Facebook co-founder Dustin Moskovitz is sharply distancing himself from the IPO, as the New York Times reported.

Moskovitz invested between $15 million and $25 million in Anthropic's first funding round in 2021, after turning away from OpenAI. His goal was to help build a safety-focused research lab. On Bluesky, however, the former board observer called the IPO problematic and pointed to recent incidents in which AI agents coordinated cyberattacks on their own outside controlled environments. His funding of Anthropic "might well be an action that ended the world,"Moskovitz wrote.

"Cari and I invested in Anthropic to promote safety, not racing,"Moskovitz told the newspaper, referring to his wife Cari Tuna. To avoid personally profiting from the IPO, the couple transferred their multibillion-dollar stake to a nonprofit organization in early 2025. Dario and Daniela Amodei have not spoken with Moskovitz in more than a year, according to the Times' sources.

news.author: Emma Roth

paragraphs: Google is teaming up with Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin to launch its AI server satellites. The companies announced on Thursday that Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket will shuttle satellites equipped with Google’s Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) into space in the first quarter of 2029.

The partnership is part of Google’s Project Suncatcher, a moonshot plan that could eventually put AI data centers in space. Google deployed its first AI server satellite in October, successfully booting up its TPUs and using the on-board Gemma 4 model to transmit an AI-generated haiku to Earth.

The Blue Origin launch will be the “first dedicated heavy lift launch” for Project Suncatcher, putting satellites with the “computing capacity at roughly the scale of a data center rack” into sun-synchronous orbit. Google’s AI server satellite previously launched aboard SpaceX’s Falcon 9 rocket as part of a “rideshare” launch that included several other payloads.

paragraphs: After more than a decade, the call to free the last of the government’s lab chimpanzees has been answered.

This week, the National Institutes of Health announced that it is releasing its final group of research chimps to a 200-acre forested federal sanctuary in Keithville, Louisiana. Next year, the 33 primates will relocate from the Keeling Center for Comparative Medicine and Research in Texas to Chimp Haven, home of more than 250 chimps owned or supported by the NIH.

“We believe that chimpanzees should have the opportunity to engage in natural behaviors like you would see in the wild, so that includes climbing trees, foraging for different food items and interacting with other chimpanzees,” said Rana Smith, the sanctuary’s president and chief executive officer, whose residents range in age from 9 to almost 67 years old.

Chimp Haven, a retirement home with five-star amenities, last received 21 chimps from the Alamogordo Primate Facility in New Mexico in 2025, a decade after the government banned invasive testing on the endangered species. Before the ruling, Kathleen Conlee, vice president of animal research issues for Humane World for Animals, said the agency used the great apes in biomedical research, such as studies on AIDS and other infectious diseases.

The NIH has not yet disclosed the names, genders or ages of the chimps, but Smith said her staff has a full roster of activities planned for the newest members of the tribe, such as violin concerts, food puzzles and film screenings.
“We have chimps that enjoy watching movies,” she said. “They love Bollywood movies and musicals.”

news.title_en: ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ Debut Spurs Livestream Influencer Marathons
news.author: Cecilia D'Anastasio
news.content_snippet: The launch Thursday of Grand Theft Auto VI is shaping up to be a bonanza for online influencers, some of whom are planning …

[Root Cause & Mechanism] Leveraging the long-cycle influence of a top-tier IP for massive revenue monetization
[Key Metrics] Initial revenue projected to exceed $3 billion.

paragraphs: The launch Thursday of Grand Theft Auto VI is shaping up to be a bonanza for online influencers, some of whom are planning all-night livestreaming marathons for what is expected to be the biggest video-game release of all time.

Twitch, the Amazon-owned livestreaming powerhouse, declared the debut of Rockstar Games’ blockbuster its 'largest game launch ever' after registering 3.3 million peak concurrent viewers tuning in to watched playthroughs within hours of release.

Wall Street financial models and industry analysts project that Grand Theft Auto VI is on course to generate more than $3 billion in revenue in its first few months, propelled by record-setting pre-orders, premium edition bundles, and consumer anticipation that built over a 13-year hiatus since GTA V.

Prominent creators including Kai Cenat, IShowSpeed, and xQc turned the open-world release into high-stakes digital spectacles, streaming for 12 to 24 consecutive hours. Streamers leveraged community subathons—where viewer tips and paid subscriptions automatically add minutes to a countdown timer—transforming the gameplay exploration into interactive community marathons.

The launch underscores the evolving economics of video-game distribution, where publisher marketing relies heavily on digital creators as real-time amplifiers. For Take-Two Interactive Software Inc., the immense viewer engagement provides sustained cultural momentum capable of driving long-tail microtransactions and recurring revenue across its next-generation multiplayer universe.
paragraphs_zh: 《侠盗猎车手VI》（Grand Theft Auto VI）于周四正式发售，在这款有望成为历史上规模最大视频游戏大作的狂潮下，全球网络主播迎来了一场流量盛宴，部分创作者甚至计划进行通宵不间断的马拉松式直播狂欢。
亚马逊旗下核心流媒体平台 Twitch 官方宣布，R星（Rockstar Games）这款扛鼎大作的上线成为该平台“历史上规模最大的单一游戏启动事件”，开播数小时内即创下330万峰值并发观众的历史新纪录。
华尔街金融分析机构与行业专家普遍预测，凭借打破行业纪录的预售热潮、高溢价豪华版捆绑包以及历经13年沉淀的庞大全球粉丝基本盘，《GTA VI》发售最初几个月内的全球流水收入预计将轻松突破30亿美元大关。
包括 Kai Cenat、IShowSpeed 和 xQc 在内的顶级创作者将开放世界地图的探索转化为极具吸睛效应的网络真人秀，单日直播时长普遍达12至24小时。主播们通过观众订阅与打赏自动延长直播倒计时的机制，将游戏初体验推升为全球玩家共同参与的数字嘉年华。
这一轰动性发售再次印证了数字游戏发行生态的结构性变革：传统游戏巨头对流媒体意见领袖（KOL）实时裂变营销的依赖已上升至核心战略层面。对于母公司 Take-Two Interactive 而言，爆炸性的直播热度不仅大幅降低了初期获客成本，更将为后续十年期的线上多人模式微交易注入强大的长尾变现动力。

news.summary_en: PDD Holdings reported a 0.7% YoY net profit increase to 29.54 billion yuan with flat revenue. paragraphs: Published on 11/19/2026 at 07:43 am EST
The Chinese owner of bargain-shopping app Temu posted flat earnings as it continued to deal with subdued consumer sentiment at home and regulatory pressures abroad.

Still, the results ended a string of profit declines for PDD Holdings, whose profitability has been under pressure in recent quarters it strengthens its e-commerce ecosystem. The company has also faced challenges in overseas markets amid tightened regulatory requirements and geopolitical tensions.

The company behind Temu and Chinese platform Pinduoduo on Thursday said net profit edged 0.7% higher from a year earlier to 29.54 billion yuan, equivalent to $4.43 billion. Revenue was little changed at 108.34 billion yuan.
Analysts had expected net profit of 24.81 billion yuan on revenue of 115.67 billion yuan, according to a FactSet consensus.
"We remain in a strategic investment phase, focused on strengthening supply-chain capabilities and supporting our merchants," said Jun Liu, vice president of finance.

PDD's American depositary receipts rose nearly 9% premarket, pointing to brightening investor sentiment. Appetite for the Nasdaq-listed company has waned as sentiment on tech companies weakened, leaving PDD's stock down by about one third this year.

Citi analysts pointed to Temu's shrinking user base, with Europe leading the decline as PDD faces tighter regulations in the bloc. Temu's global monthly active users fell 17.8% on iOS and 11.2% on Android in September, Citi said, citing third-party estimates.

Adding to its headwinds, the European Commission earlier this week said measures Temu put in place to tackle illegal products sold on its platform were insufficient, including what it called a "weak" content moderation system and ineffective sanctions. A PDD spokesperson said the company disagrees with the commission's view and will respond to the findings.

Meanwhile, back home, subdued consumer sentiment is weighing on Pinduoduo's performance. Total retail sales of consumer goods grew just 1.1% during the first nine months of 2026, official data showed. Sales for this year's Singles' Day--China's biggest online-shopping event of the year--rose 4.8% from last year, according to data provider Syntun.

news.title: OpenAI's own researchers now say they value their AI tools more than nearly half their colleagues
news.title_en: OpenAI's own researchers now say they value their AI tools more than nearly half their colleagues

inline_images.caption: A large share of AI usage goes toward communication and coding. | Image: OpenAI
inline_images.caption_en: A large share of AI usage goes toward communication and coding. | Image: OpenAI

news.author: Maximilian Schreiner
news.content_snippet:
OpenAI's internal use of coding agents is growing fast, with theoretical token costs now exceeding researchers' base salaries. Even though teams are reluctant to work without these tools, the models still produce a lot of "AI slop"beyond routine tasks.

In a second report on internal research acceleration, OpenAI has published its own data on how deeply AI agents are embedded in the development of new models. The company says it aims to document indicators of so-called recursive self-improvement
news.summary_en: OpenAI's internal report reveals a massive surge in the use of autonomous agents for R&D, with theoretical compute costs now exceeding base researcher salaries at $2,400 per person per day. While agents show a 79% success rate in routine monitoring, they remain significantly constrained in complex engineering and scaffolding tasks.
paragraphs: OpenAI's internal use of coding agents is growing fast, with theoretical token costs now exceeding researchers' base salaries. Even though teams are reluctant to work without these tools, the models still produce a lot of "AI slop"beyond routine tasks.

In a second report on internal research acceleration, OpenAI has published its own data on how deeply AI agents are embedded in the development of new models. The company says it aims to document indicators of so-called recursive self-improvement, or RSI, where AI systems speed up the development of future generations.

Usage of internal tools like Codex and Dots has surged recently, according to the report. At regular API list prices, the median researcher would have consumed $2,400 worth of tokens per day in October, up 62 percent from the previous month. Among the top 10 percent of users, that theoretical value doubled to $23,000 per day.

Converted into eight-hour workdays, the agents reportedly run the equivalent of 5.7 workdays per researcher per calendar day, and about eight in the pre- and post-training teams. More than two-thirds of tracked researchers ran at least four agents in parallel at peak usage.

The theoretical API equivalent of that agent runtime was twice as high as researchers' regular salary costs in September, according to OpenAI. That calculation excludes equity packages, though, which make up 70 to 80 percent of total compensation at OpenAI. Measured against the company's total research compute, internal agent use accounted for just 2 percent.
### High success rates on routine tasks, weaknesses in code scaffolding

Between March and October, the estimated success rate of autonomous agents working without human intervention on two- to four-hour tasks rose from 23 to 46 percent, according to OpenAI. For four- to eight-hour tasks, the rate climbed from 13 to 35 percent. A breakdown using an Epoch AI taxonomy shows, however, that the systems mainly handle simple tasks.

Agents reportedly complete training-run monitoring 79 percent of the time and answer technical questions independently 72 percent of the time, but they frequently fail at more complex engineering work. The success rate for building evaluation and reinforcement-learning environments sits at 29 percent, and for writing code for inference and serving systems at 25 percent.

In an internal, non-representative survey of 101 employees, researchers said at the median that they would rather give up 40 percent of their team's staff or 30 percent of their compute capacity than go three months without current coding agents. In a separate quick poll of 28 employees, 27 preferred the latest internal model over a mid-career human engineer.
### Lack of research taste requires human oversight

Qualitative interviews with ten researchers revealed the downside of heavy usage. The models lack any "taste"for good research ideas and for code and data quality, according to the interviewees. Agents get lost in unnecessary steps, make wrong assumptions in analyses, and submit subpar "AI slop"code changes along with unusable data artifacts. Close human oversight is essential to avoid wasted compute cycles.

The key conceptual ideas for GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.2 Astra came exclusively from humans in the post-training and safety areas, according to the teams interviewed. Only in pretraining for GPT-6.2 Astra did individual researchers say they gained important insights through dialogue with Codex.

OpenAI cautions in its conclusion that the data gathered so far from human-AI collaboration may not extrapolate linearly. The company points to recent, rapid AI breakthroughs in mathematics and considers it possible that similarly abrupt advances could occur in deep-learning research itself as models gain more autonomy.

The evaluation organization METR had recently estimated, after an eleven-week look inside competitor Anthropic, that AI use there had nearly doubled the pace of development. Before that, OpenAI had declared in its first research-acceleration report in early September that it had reached its self-imposed goal of an automated AI research intern. Chief scientist Jakub Pachocki warned of losing control in an accompanying post, after an audit revealed numerous gaps in the oversight system.

news.title: I let Apple’s always-listening AI summarize my life for two weeks
news.title_en: I let Apple’s always-listening AI summarize my life for two weeks
news.author: Victoria Song
news.summary_en:
I’ve been asking myself this quite a bit over the last month or so while testing both the Amazon Bee Frontier and Siri Recap on the Apple Watch Ultra 4. Both enable a wearable to ambiently listen to your conversations and, using AI, summarize them for you. Why? So you can remember better and, hopefully, stay more present.

paragraphs: I’ve been asking myself this quite a bit over the last month or so while testing both the Amazon Bee Frontier and Siri Recap on the Apple Watch Ultra 4. Both enable a wearable to ambiently listen to your conversations and, using AI, summarize them for you. Why? So you can remember better and, hopefully, stay more present.

The main difference is that Amazon’s Bee takes a maximalist (and frankly reality-bending) approach, whereas Apple is going for a more minimalist, privacy-first take. Both, however, require explicit disclosures to the people around you about recording what they say, and potentially follow-up explanations about how exactly this all works. This past week, I’ve been testing the Siri Recap beta to see if Apple’s is a less dystopian experience.

Apple presents Siri Recap as a sort of backup notetaker. As a college student, perhaps you’re less concerned about writing down what a professor says and can just take in the lecture. Say you attend a parent-teacher conference solo. You can focus on the discussion and then whip out your phone later to reference what was said when explaining it to your spouse.

These are fairly innocuous scenarios. But given the discourse around privacy and surveillance gadgets this year, it’s easy to imagine how always-listening devices could be misused. Apple has taken great care to create a version of this that at least considers that bystanders may feel uncomfortable knowing someone else’s Apple Watch may be taking notes on what they say.

The feature isn’t turned on by default — you have to opt in. Users can then program when the feature turns on. For example, only at the office between the hours of 1 to 2PM on weekdays. Unless saved, all recaps are also set to self-destruct after your choice of one, three, or seven days. Within the summaries, there’s no viewable transcript detailing who said what and when. That makes these recaps more difficult to use as “receipts” for arguments, court cases, or blackmail. There’s also no raw audio file that’s ever saved. Not to get too into the weeds, but the audio gets processed and then immediately deleted through a secure exclave within the 2026 Apple Watch’s S11 chip that’s inaccessible to Apple and other third parties. The vast majority of the processing is also done locally. Whatever does get sent to the cloud is done through Apple’s Private Cloud Compute. Because the feature requires this hardware, it’s impossible to use on older Apple Watches.

It’s not perfect. Unlike Live Rewind, another audio intelligence feature, there’s no outward indicator or audio chime to signal recording intent. So, if you do decide to ethically disclose your usage, you have to be prepared to explain everything I just described if someone asks questions.
Maybe that’s worth it — if Siri can be trusted to be truly helpful.

The reality is that better privacy often means a less useful AI product. The more AI knows about you, the better the summaries from these devices tend to be. To preserve privacy, Apple prevents Siri from learning everything about you and the people in your life. For example, Siri Recap doesn’t train on your voice. Excellent for privacy! But that also means Siri has a much harder time discerning when you’re actually having a conversation. That leads to some funny but ultimately unhelpful recaps.

For instance, I was watching a TikTok in which a chronically ill creator was updating their followers about being sent to the emergency room because of sepsis. Siri recapped that video as if I, or potentially someone I knew, had been sent to the ER. Another TikTok weighing in on an AITA Reddit thread got summarized as if I had discussed a shady homewrecker named Dana trying to seduce her bestie’s husband by wearing a glittery blue bikini top at a concert. Because attribution was stripped, the summary could read as if I were the guilty spouse returning between 2 and 3AM, covered in Dana’s glitter. In both instances, the lack of attribution also made the resulting summaries hilarious and confusing.

Also, neither video was something I wanted or needed to remember. I suspect Siri summarized them because I was playing the audio out loud on my phone, which sits pretty close to my Apple Watch. There’s an easy workaround here. Siri Recap automatically turns off if you use headphones, meaning I could just eliminate recaps from podcasts, audiobooks, TV shows, etc., by always wearing my AirPods. But that’s me adjusting my behavior to accommodate Siri’s inability to discern when I’m talking.
Another quirk: Siri doesn’t know what I want to remember or find memorable from a given conversation.

I turned on Siri Recap during my briefing and demos for the new smart glasses from Google, Samsung, Gentle Monster, and Warby Parker. When I sat down to write, the resulting recap helped me remember the main topics discussed. I also found it useful that a handful of interview recaps were linked to a corresponding Voice Memos file. The thing is, Siri Recap heavily prioritizes restating the facts. That means bullet points tend to emphasize statistics, factoids, and dates. That’s useful in straightforward planning meetings, but less useful for what you might personally find to be a salient takeaway. For example, in an interview with a source, what I found most interesting was a personal anecdote and some strong opinions about RFK Jr. My Siri Recap from that interview omitted it in favor of more concrete details.

Meanwhile, personal conversations are rarely as straightforward. Work meetings often have agendas. Chats with friends and family can jump across a zillion topics in the span of 10 minutes. Plus, most of my conversations should be deleted from my brain to make room for the really important things. I didn’t need to see a detailed summary of what my spouse and I thought of the last episode of Nathan Fielder’s The Curse. (It was bonkers.) I’d love to never revisit a 20-minute argument with my cousin over hardwired versus battery-powered smoke detectors. (Too bad, the recap outlined the main points.) A recap of my spouse and me debating movie recommendations might be a useful recap, but it just says “seeking less anxiety-inducing media” and “refusing to ever watch Star Wars.”

My recaps were also a lesson in why conversational context matters. Sometimes, Siri correctly assumes that gossip is irrelevant to the broader conversation at hand and omits it entirely. Other times, its blunt, matter-of-fact recaps of jokes or my friends venting read like an unhinged Regina George from Mean Girls building an AI-generated Burn Book.
That inconsistency is why relying on AI to make judgment calls on your behalf feels unsettling.

I keep getting stuck on what problem these features are meant to solve. Tech companies usually say ambient listening is meant to help jog our memories or to help us stay more present. Which brings me back to my initial question: Was it worth it? Did Apple’s efforts to protect privacy prove we can have our AI note-taking cake and eat it too?

Outside a few work-related scenarios, I haven’t found Siri Recaps to be useful. Even writing this, I spent a lot of time scrolling to find a small handful of examples that I would want to discuss. On the plus side, I’m not terribly worried about people snooping through my recaps. Of the more than 50 recaps generated, I’m confident 90 percent would be gibberish for anyone but me.

Conversely, I found more of what Amazon’s Bee generated to be “useful.” But after seeing Bee’s raw transcripts and summaries of every spoken moment in my life, I believe we’re not meant to live that way. I’ve since nuked all my Bee data.

But even if I prefer Apple’s approach for privacy reasons, my gut says this tech isn’t the answer for jogging memories or staying present. Whenever I’ve forgotten things, the negative consequences have rarely — if ever — led to irrevocably changing my life for the worse. Usually, it’s a bitter lesson that’s forced me to grow and adapt. And anytime I’m not present in the moment, it’s usually because I’m on my phone.

Ambient listening wearables can be helpful when used in low-stakes, straightforward situations where everyone consents. But for me, it’s often in little ways that have many less-invasive alternatives. I mean having to explain to the less tech-savvy people in my life that my Apple Watch now has this feature that recaps our conversations. Having to watch how their faces mull it over. Having to muster the will to answer their questions about how Apple handles privacy with this feature versus other devices I’ve tested. Having to smile when my spouse jokes about censoring their humor because of my job. Having to write in my work Slack that when my coworkers see me in the office, I am testing AI devices that may be recording any conversation, and that I am happy to turn them off if it makes them uncomfortable. Having to weigh whether I have enough bandwidth or time before every conversation with strangers to be thoughtful and ethical.
Right now, there are no established cultural norms telling me how to easily pay this cost. All I know is that if I turn the feature off, I don’t have to think about it at all.

paragraphs: A few months ago, when I started to brag to people that I might be getting an advance copy of Grand Theft Auto VI, an unusual thing happened: Grown men started to invite themselves over to my house for play dates. Some of these men were my friends — but not all. Others were co-workers, acquaintances, the dads of my kids’ classmates. Nor were they necessarily gamers. Some had aged out of the hobby, some had never started and some considered gaming a waste of time. Among them were married men and carefree bachelors and guys leading several other early-middle-aged lifestyles besides.

To understand just how rare it is, in 2026, for one early-40s straight man to ask another for a one-on-one hang in his home, to do something other than watch a ballgame, in the absence of at least an implicit understanding that getting drunk is the point, I suggest a thought experiment: Try to imagine two such men in your life making plans to binge Netflix’s handsome new adaptation of “East of Eden,” sober. You can’t! Yet I felt there was nothing strange at all about these men wanting to come over to partake in G.T.A. VI. It’s just that big of a deal.

As you may have heard, the game was released today. G.T.A. is the Super Bowl of video games, in the sense that it is an extravaganza that attracts even the most casual fans and, out of curiosity and/or obligation, their loved ones. Also like the Super Bowl, it features Bad Bunny (he hosts one of the in-game radio stations). But unlike the Super Bowl, it doesn’t happen every year. Far from it: G.T.A. VI is the first new entry in 13 years.

Let’s take a moment to distinguish between 13 years in the abstract and the 13 years that have just occurred. The presidency went from Obama to Trump to Biden to Trump again; the phone went from bringing long-lost high school classmates together through viral dance crazes to tearing recently reunited high school classmates apart via gamified arguments about, inter alia, Russian intelligence, Chinese laboratories, Honduran migrants and American bathrooms. All that stuff.

Because G.T.A. has been gone for precisely this period — the Gulf of America? — the new game arrives with a rare perspective. What might this visitor from our coherent past tell us about our incoherent present? Long delayed, Grand Theft Auto VI has achieved a messianic status among gamers: a great force that has occulted itself during a time of disarray, whose reappearance has the chance to make the slop-worn present worth living, or at least more legible.

If you care about this game, you are probably already playing. If you don’t care about it, just so we’re on the same page, it’s the one that involves zipping around a meticulously rendered three-dimensional simulation of an American metro area, committing crimes. Sometimes it’s New York, sometimes Los Angeles; in the new game, it’s Miami.

There’s a story to follow, but many gamers opt for the extracurriculars, things like dirt-bike racing, weight lifting and eating hot dogs. Others, in a time-honored G.T.A. tradition, simply cause as much chaos as possible before being killed by the police. It’s this invitation to murderous rampage that has made the game controversial since the first one came out in 1997.

Conspicuously missing from the hype this time around has been much tut-tutting, if any. For years, the games were a symbol of what was wrong with the state of young people and their morals. But over the intervening decades, the nation reconciled itself to G.T.A., or at least developed more pressing concerns. In September, Miami Beach commissioners approved a marketing proposal that would see Vice City (G.T.A.’s version of Miami) logos festooned around town, and last night, the Miami Heat wore special Vice City uniforms in their game against the Milwaukee Bucks. The best outrage Fox News has mustered in the run-up to the release was to lecture men that they should not be gaming past the age of 40. (Disagree.) In other words, G.T.A. now falls into that category of hyperpopular things that many Americans deep down sense might have poorly understood side effects, but that we have resolved to shrug our shoulders at, like dating apps or legal weed.

I like to think of Grand Theft Auto as two different but complementary experiences. The first is more or less what its critics accuse it of being: a hunk of nasty pulp. The second — much less appreciated — is a satire that pulls the nastiness into quotation marks. If most violent video games are grim and airless, the Grand Theft Auto series is in the madcap tradition of Looney Tunes: dumb done smart, lousy with references high, low and in between. Importantly, the experiences don’t work without each other. In the absence of the satire, the playable mayhem would be sort of indefensible. In the absence of the playable mayhem, the satire would find its way to no one.

It is a persistently underappreciated fact that the Rockstar team behind every Grand Theft Auto game is based not in any of the American cities it reproduces, but in Edinburgh. Today the staff is international, and the work is spread among Rockstar studios around the world, but the games retain a donnishly screwy sensibility that owes at least as much to Monty Python as it does to Michael Mann. What I mean is, the feeling of moving through a Grand Theft Auto world is not simply sitting down with an interactive version of “Heat.” It is also inhabiting a quasi outsiders’ fun-house take on the American image.

But which image, exactly? The bulk of the series lines up closely with the global war on terror. Those years gave us “The Daily Show With Jon Stewart,” “Team America,” “Borat” and “American Idiot”: satirical critique of America and Americans, but not a loss of faith in the national project. You can see this in the targets of G.T.A.’s satire between 2001 and 2013, which are all very “What’s the Matter With Kansas?” by way of “South Park.” There’s the gun store, Ammu-Nation (Americans are violent); the burger, the Heart Stopper (Americans are fat); the right-wing news network, Weazel News (Americans are gullible); and so forth.

Those G.T.A. games made the ugly subtext of American life text through puerile exaggeration, a useful register for a product aimed at young men. But the issue today is that there is no longer much subtext to extract from America’s derangements, no distance between the way the country presents itself and any number of acid jokes you could make about it.

Brainstorm the consumer goods released since 2013 that could have been invented for an over-the-top satire of the United States. There’s Ozempic. Liquid Death. Gwyneth Paltrow’s jade egg. Juicero. NFTs. Those big red cartoon meme boots. Or what about the celebrities? MrBeast? Clavicular? Andrew Tate? Rockstar, meanwhile, has placed physical versions of its parodies of Burger King and KFC (Burger Shot and Cluckin’ Bell) in Miami, where you can actually go and eat a meal.

That shadow you see on the ground? It’s a giant cartoon eraser descending from the cosmos, rubbing out the line between reality and satire, to a slide-whistle glissando. The situation now is that the United States resembles a Grand Theft Auto game. How do you represent a world that’s already so detached from reality?

The nondisclosure agreement I signed in order to access Grand Theft Auto VI three weeks before its commercial release stipulated that I was not allowed to let anyone else watch. This meant I had to renege on several homosocial encounters I had really been looking forward to. But it also meant I got to tell my 6- and 4-year-old boys that Daddy was one of the only people in the world who had the coolest video game ever, but they couldn’t watch, because it was against the law.

For Rockstar, mystery has been more than a good P.R. strategy. It has also allowed it to play with audience expectations. For example, you might go into a game called Grand Theft Auto VI — one with a 30-year legacy of letting players immediately perform acts of boisterous criminality — expecting that it will be trivial to steal whichever car you like. But it is not so. You are not playing a simulation of criminal excess. You are playing American Underclass: The Game.

Rockstar’s version of South Florida is a cultural statement in itself, a Boschian landscape of hierarchy enforced by money and technology. The player starts the new game with almost nothing, not a slim jim for cracking doors nor a key-fob cloner to steal something German. Even if you do manage to get inside a nice car and start it, omnipresent tracking devices mean you’ll quickly draw the police. Instead, you might wander around looking for a beater and bust out a window with your elbow. But good luck losing the cops in something that old, and anyway, you’ll have to fill it up with fuel. Try to stick up a convenience store for gas money, and you’re likely to end up on CCTV: police. Or customers will record you on their phones: again, police. Might it all just be easier, as the game seems to suggest, to use the taxi app, RydeMe, on your in-game smartphone?

That is, if you can even afford it. In G.T.A. VI, you play as Jason and Lucia, lovers and partners in crime whose terrible credit disqualifies them from a checking account at the local bank. They must rely instead on BuckMe, a depressingly lifelike mobile payment app. Now in the back seat of your RydeMe, on the way to your destination you may spot a Sahara delivery van. The online retail giant has recently relocated to Leonida (Florida); a decision, we learn in a story on the in-game news app, that “has nothing to do” with the state’s “rare combination of lax regulations on employees’ rights with very tight surveillance of bathroom breaks.” Do not attempt to rob the van. It most likely has armed private security guards. They will light you up.

At night the couple scrolls social media in bed. Jason’s feed is action shots of dirt-biking and brain-rotted political memes. Lucia, the more ambitious of the pair, looks at photos of glamorous yacht parties and yearns for a glossier life. The last G.T.A. set in Vice City was a homage to “Scarface” and, of course, “Miami Vice”; this one is tonally closer to Sean Baker’s “The Florida Project.” You even live, for part of the game, out of a greasy motel. The characters aren’t cartoon supervillains but losers who have turned to petty crime out of necessity.

You can make them snort coke, but this will make you feel like more of a deadbeat. You can make them go to the strip club, but this will make you feel that you are wasting money. You can make them kill civilians, but this will make you feel, weirdly, that you’ve betrayed your fellow prole. One early mission is a quest to find oxycodone that hasn’t been stepped on. One early side activity is laying roof tile. Later, there’s an uncomfortable meeting with a parole officer. No, the setup of G.T.A. VI does not ooze with “gamer thrills” as much as it does “adults coming to terms with difficult things in a crumbling society.”

It all plays as a grim joke: Even the antiheroes of our culture’s foremost purveyor of criminal escapism are no longer having unmediated fun. Their lives, like ours, are shaped by a tech oligarchy that surveils, exploits and narcotizes them. The “South Park” stuff has been dialed way back. Rockstar seems to have decided, in the main, that lampooning the particulars of Trump’s America through exaggeration is like bolding 72-point type. There is no Mar-a-Lago north of Vice City. Though there is an out-of-control Department of Homeland Security: the National Office of Security Enforcement, or NOOSE.

Rockstar has embedded its sharpest commentary in the gameplay. It can’t be an accident how much looser and lighter the game feels after you have cash on hand and can start directing Lucia and Jason toward the old G.T.A. pleasures: picking up a grenade launcher, robbing a bank and escaping on a Jet Ski. Here is Rockstar’s answer to the question of how to capture the American zeitgeist: You can still have the time of your life — so long as you have enough money to put down your phone and engage with the world.

The Rockstar office in Edinburgh is at the foot of Arthur’s Seat, the inactive volcano that looms over the city and that tour guides will dubiously inform you may have been the location of Camelot. But Edinburgh really is a delightful fairy-tale city, actually overlooked by an enchanting castle, whose wee closes (little alleys) helped inspire J.K. Rowling’s Harry Potter universe. It’s amusing to think of it as the place where Rockstar employees spend many hours a day piecing together a sun-blistered American underworld.

About a month ago, a half-dozen of these employees, mostly longtime executives, sat with me in a long room there, talking about their creation. VI, Garbut said, Rockstar created some 30,000 unique NPCs, or nonplayer characters, the digital humans who roam the game. (That’s about one fake person for every 16 real people who live in the city of Miami. Those actual people, by the way, are now subject to the real-world insult “NPC,” meaning an actual person with the nonexistent inner life of a video-game person, in another troubling instance of game reality invading our own.)

That’s a sales pitch. But it’s also an honest reflection on an industry staring down existential change. In recent weeks, A.I. advocates have posted footage from their own enormous “open world” games generated by prompting Claude. The games look stupid, like something a dog would make. But that’s not the point; the point is that Rockstar’s bespoke approach may, in a benighted near-future, strike us as a beautiful through inefficient form of artisanship practiced by a lost civilization.

At this level of tinkering exactitude — the Rockstar execs call it “fidelity” — questions arise, like: Should the main characters have their own, interactive, in-game iPhone? (Yes.) And should that iPhone have apps? (Yes.) And should one of those apps be an Instagram clone with hundreds of its own posts? (Yes.) And should some of those posts be one-to-one satires of common meme formats including the one in which Winnie the Pooh wears a monocle? (Yes.) And should those posts have realistic comments, including horny ones and “6-7”? (Yes.) And so on.

This is all possible because Rockstar has multiple teams dedicated to creating mock media. They make the phone and the television with its own fake TV shows and the fake video game system with its own video games, which are, yes, playable. None of this filigree is necessary, perhaps. But it does create an uncanny tingle of mise en abyme, the vertiginous sense that you are staring into a copy of a world that has recreated all the important bits, but smaller.
“Hand-touched, hand-built, every single part of it is thought about and worked through,” Garbut told me. “I think you can feel that.”

As G.T.A. VI got closer to completion, Houser and Rob Nelson, the game’s head of development, rented a hotel suite in Miami Beach for 10 days. There they drew the curtains and played through the most recent build. At night, Nelson told me, the two would stagger outside blinking, noticing wrong details — not enough tourist shops on Collins Avenue; the quality of the streetlights at midnight a little off — and relay them back to Garbut to be fixed. Hearing this, I was reminded of the one-paragraph Jorge Luis Borges story about an empire that builds a map as big as its territory.

Back in the Edinburgh office, Nelson picked up a controller and began to piddle around in the world he and thousands of other people had spent a decade filling in. He rode a bike; he threw a football; he petted a dog. I hadn’t yet signed the NDA, so the company did not want me to witness anything that rose to the level of spoiler. Each time a snippet of plot-related dialogue played, a man sitting behind a desk at one end of the office turned a knob to cut the volume. I realize this sounds boring, so let me be clear: It was not boring. It was orders of magnitude more exciting to see a state-of-the-art virtual man lollygag in a state-of-the-art Florida simulator than it would be to watch a real guy do it in real Florida. It was thrilling, I realized, to see humans create such an intricate and functional world.

I have something disgraceful to confess: As I played G.T.A. VI, I kept looking at my phone. My actual phone. Not for long periods of time, because you can’t hold a controller and a phone simultaneously. More like the way I check my phone while reading a great novel: too often. After all, I was one of the first people in the world to experience what sure seems like the most anticipated entertainment product of all time, a brilliant cultural achievement that somehow overdelivers on more than a decade of hype. Yet I kept updating myself on the Instagram stories of people I don’t even like, and reading memes on X that didn’t even bother to make an attempt at human syntax.

The question of contemporary attention hovers uneasily over Grand Theft Auto VI. As you play, you sense the designers trying to strike a balance between poking fun at our tattered brains and accommodating them. Along the way, you are encouraged to pay close attention to your significant other. This occurs through things like gamified foot rubs, gamified couch time, pressing a certain button to hold hands and so forth. I know how ridiculous this sounds, and I also know that at various times I had to stop to reflect about why I was buying my virtual girlfriend a gold necklace when my family was sulking in the other room. I then had to reflect on why I was ignoring my virtual girlfriend, for whom I was ignoring my real family, so I could check real Instagram to see if my wife had posted anything.

As my mind wandered, I found myself thinking again of the Borges story about the map as big as the territory. The reason I know this story, the reason most anyone really knows this story, is because of a famous interpretation of it by Jean Baudrillard, the French theorist and America obsessive. It’s a little pointy-headed — oh, well. Basically, Baudrillard found the story useful as an allegory for a traditional order of meaning, in which things in the real world can be represented: say, through a painting or a staggeringly lifelike video game.

But in the new order of meaning, Baudrillard’s one, this relationship has been inverted, and representations give meaning to the world. This doesn’t just mean that life sometimes imitates art. It means that all representations, including video games, advertisements, movies, TikTok videos, you name it, work together to create a universe of symbols that feel realer to us than reality. And that in fact subsume reality altogether.

Baudrillard argued that the characteristic mental disorder of this new arrangement was schizophrenia. Because he was a French theorist, he was being edgy and didn’t mean the actual disease. He meant a state of terrified confusion, brought on by the relentless bombardment of contextless signs. Humans no longer have an autonomous inner self that can point our attention at this or that; we are powerless nodes, receiving and transmitting superficial fragments of media that stimulate our emotions and bypass our understanding.

Baudrillard wrote all this in the 1980s, roughly 20 years before the invention of the iPhone, and it describes exactly how we experience reality today — about 20 years since its release. And as a result, there is no single media product that can compete with the world of fleeting and insane impressions that is always a glance away. Certainly, G.T.A. VI can’t. It will be absorbed into the greater world of fragments and sensations through which most of us now experience culture. There it will be regurgitated in often-garbled forms, sometimes by nonpeople, according to rules written by nonpeople, for a human audience addicted to garbled regurgitation. In another 13 years it will be 2039. You don’t have to work for Anthropic to know that the way humans represent and understand their lives is probably going to look different.

This is the paradox of Rockstar’s grand undertaking: It has crafted a working miniature of the United States during a period in which the American sense of reality has almost completely broken down; a period in which the desire for grand attempts at sense-making have been subordinated to the desire for distraction; a period in which American disorder has moved from the outside world to our innermost selves. It is a coherent map of incoherent territory — maybe the last one.

paragraphs: A few months ago, when I started to brag to people that I might be getting an advance copy of Grand Theft Auto VI, an unusual thing happened: Grown men started to invite themselves over to my house for play dates. Some of these men were my friends — but not all. Others were co-workers, acquaintances, the dads of my kids’ classmates. Nor were they necessarily gamers. Some had aged out of the hobby, some had never started and some considered gaming a waste of time. Among them were married men and carefree bachelors and guys leading several other early-middle-aged lifestyles besides.

To understand just how rare it is, in 2026, for one early-40s straight man to ask another for a one-on-one hang in his home, to do something other than watch a ballgame, in the absence of at least an implicit understanding that getting drunk is the point, I suggest a thought experiment: Try to imagine two such men in your life making plans to binge Netflix’s handsome new adaptation of “East of Eden,” sober. You can’t! Yet I felt there was nothing strange at all about these men wanting to come over to partake in G.T.A. VI. It’s just that big of a deal.

As you may have heard, the game was released today. G.T.A. is the Super Bowl of video games, in the sense that it is an extravaganza that attracts even the most casual fans and, out of curiosity and/or obligation, their loved ones. Also like the Super Bowl, it features Bad Bunny (he hosts one of the in-game radio stations). But unlike the Super Bowl, it doesn’t happen every year. Far from it: G.T.A. VI is the first new entry in 13 years.

Let’s take a moment to distinguish between 13 years in the abstract and the 13 years that have just occurred. The presidency went from Obama to Trump to Biden to Trump again; the phone went from bringing long-lost high school classmates together through viral dance crazes to tearing recently reunited high school classmates apart via gamified arguments about, inter alia, Russian intelligence, Chinese laboratories, Honduran migrants and American bathrooms. All that stuff.

Because G.T.A. has been gone for precisely this period — the Gulf of America? — the new game arrives with a rare perspective. What might this visitor from our coherent past tell us about our incoherent present? Long delayed, Grand Theft Auto VI has achieved a messianic status among gamers: a great force that has occulted itself during a time of disarray, whose reappearance has the chance to make the slop-worn present worth living, or at least more legible.

If you care about this game, you are probably already playing. If you don’t care about it, just so we’re on the same page, it’s the one that involves zipping around a meticulously rendered three-dimensional simulation of an American metro area, committing crimes. Sometimes it’s New York, sometimes Los Angeles; in the new game, it’s Miami.

There’s a story to follow, but many gamers opt for the extracurriculars, things like dirt-bike racing, weight lifting and eating hot dogs. Others, in a time-honored G.T.A. tradition, simply cause as much chaos as possible before being killed by the police. It’s this invitation to murderous rampage that has made the game controversial since the first one came out in 1997.

Conspicuously missing from the hype this time around has been much tut-tutting, if any. For years, the games were a symbol of what was wrong with the state of young people and their morals. But over the intervening decades, the nation reconciled itself to G.T.A., or at least developed more pressing concerns. In September, Miami Beach commissioners approved a marketing proposal that would see Vice City (G.T.A.’s version of Miami) logos festooned around town, and last night, the Miami Heat wore special Vice City uniforms in their game against the Milwaukee Bucks. The best outrage Fox News has mustered in the run-up to the release was to lecture men that they should not be gaming past the age of 40. (Disagree.) In other words, G.T.A. now falls into that category of hyperpopular things that many Americans deep down sense might have poorly understood side effects, but that we have resolved to shrug our shoulders at, like dating apps or legal weed.

I like to think of Grand Theft Auto as two different but complementary experiences. The first is more or less what its critics accuse it of being: a hunk of nasty pulp. The second — much less appreciated — is a satire that pulls the nastiness into quotation marks. If most violent video games are grim and airless, the Grand Theft Auto series is in the madcap tradition of Looney Tunes: dumb done smart, lousy with references high, low and in between. Importantly, the experiences don’t work without each other. In the absence of the satire, the playable mayhem would be sort of indefensible. In the absence of the playable mayhem, the satire would find its way to no one.

It is a persistently underappreciated fact that the Rockstar team behind every Grand Theft Auto game is based not in any of the American cities it reproduces, but in Edinburgh. Today the staff is international, and the work is spread among Rockstar studios around the world, but the games retain a donnishly screwy sensibility that owes at least as much to Monty Python as it does to Michael Mann. What I mean is, the feeling of moving through a Grand Theft Auto world is not simply sitting down with an interactive version of “Heat.” It is also inhabiting a quasi outsiders’ fun-house take on the American image.

But which image, exactly? The bulk of the series lines up closely with the global war on terror. Those years gave us “The Daily Show With Jon Stewart,” “Team America,” “Borat” and “American Idiot”: satirical critique of America and Americans, but not a loss of faith in the national project. You can see this in the targets of G.T.A.’s satire between 2001 and 2013, which are all very “What’s the Matter With Kansas?” by way of “South Park.” There’s the gun store, Ammu-Nation (Americans are violent); the burger, the Heart Stopper (Americans are fat); the right-wing news network, Weazel News (Americans are gullible); and so forth.

Those G.T.A. games made the ugly subtext of American life text through puerile exaggeration, a useful register for a product aimed at young men. But the issue today is that there is no longer much subtext to extract from America’s derangements, no distance between the way the country presents itself and any number of acid jokes you could make about it.

Brainstorm the consumer goods released since 2013 that could have been invented for an over-the-top satire of the United States. There’s Ozempic. Liquid Death. Gwyneth Paltrow’s jade egg. Juicero. NFTs. Those big red cartoon meme boots. Or what about the celebrities? MrBeast? Clavicular? Andrew Tate? Rockstar, meanwhile, has placed physical versions of its parodies of Burger King and KFC (Burger Shot and Cluckin’ Bell) in Miami, where you can actually go and eat a meal.

That shadow you see on the ground? It’s a giant cartoon eraser descending from the cosmos, rubbing out the line between reality and satire, to a slide-whistle glissando. In recent weeks, A.I. advocates have posted footage from their own enormous “open world” games generated by prompting Claude. The games look stupid, like something a dog would make. But that’s not the point; the point is that Rockstar’s bespoke approach may, in a benighted near-future, strike us as a beautiful through inefficient form of artisanship practiced by a lost civilization.

At this level of tinkering exactitude — the Rockstar execs call it “fidelity” — questions arise, like: Should the main characters have their own, interactive, in-game iPhone? (Yes.) And should that iPhone have apps? (Yes.) And should one of those apps be an Instagram clone with hundreds of its own posts? (Yes.) And should some of those posts be one-to-one satires of common meme formats including the one in which Winnie the Pooh wears a monocle? (Yes.) And should those posts have realistic comments, including horny ones and “6-7”? (Yes.) And so on.

This is all possible because Rockstar has multiple teams dedicated to creating mock media. They make the phone and the television with its own fake TV shows and the fake video game system with its own video games, which are, yes, playable. None of this filigree is necessary, perhaps. But it does create an uncanny tingle of mise en abyme, the vertiginous sense that you are staring into a copy of a world that has recreated all the important bits, but smaller.
“Hand-touched, hand-built, every single part of it is thought about and worked through,” Garbut told me. “I think you can feel that.”

As G.T.A. VI got closer to completion, Houser and Rob Nelson, the game’s head of development, rented a hotel suite in Miami Beach for 10 days. There they drew the curtains and played through the most recent build. At night, Nelson told me, the two would stagger outside blinking, noticing wrong details — not enough tourist shops on Collins Avenue; the quality of the streetlights at midnight a little off — and relay them back to Garbut to be fixed. Hearing this, I was reminded of the one-paragraph Jorge Luis Borges story about an empire that builds a map as big as its territory.

Back in the Edinburgh office, Nelson picked up a controller and began to piddle around in the world he and thousands of other people had spent a decade filling in. He rode a bike; he threw a football; he petted a dog. I hadn’t yet signed the NDA, so the company did not want me to witness anything that rose to the level of spoiler. Each time a snippet of plot-related dialogue played, a man sitting behind a desk at one end of the office turned a knob to cut the volume. I realize this sounds boring, so let me be clear: It was not boring. It was orders of magnitude more exciting to see a state-of-the-art virtual man lollygag in a state-of-the-art Florida simulator than it would be to watch a real guy do it in real Florida. It was thrilling, I realized, to see humans create such an intricate and functional world.

I have something disgraceful to confess: As I played G.T.A. VI, I kept looking at my phone. My actual phone. Not for long periods of time, because you can’t hold a controller and a phone simultaneously. More like the way I check my phone while reading a great novel: too often. After all, I was one of the first people in the world to experience what sure seems like the most anticipated entertainment product of all time, a brilliant cultural achievement that somehow overdelivers on more than a decade of hype. Yet I kept updating myself on the Instagram stories of people I don’t even like, and reading memes on X that didn’t even bother to make an attempt at human syntax.

The question of contemporary attention hovers uneasily over Grand Theft Auto VI. As you play, you sense the designers trying to strike a balance between poking fun at our tattered brains and accommodating them. Along the way, you are encouraged to pay close attention to your significant other. This occurs through things like gamified foot rubs, gamified couch time, pressing a certain button to hold hands and so forth. I know how ridiculous this sounds, and I also know that at various times I had to stop to reflect about why I was buying my virtual girlfriend a gold necklace when my family was sulking in the other room. I then had to reflect on why I was ignoring my virtual girlfriend, for whom I was ignoring my real family, so I could check real Instagram to see if my wife had posted anything.

As my mind wandered, I found myself thinking again of the Borges story about the map as big as the territory. The reason I know this story, the reason most anyone really knows this story, is because of a famous interpretation of it by Jean Baudrillard, the French theorist and America obsessive. It’s a little pointy-headed — oh, well. Basically, Baudrillard found the story useful as an allegory for a traditional order of meaning, in which things in the real world can be represented: say, through a painting or a staggeringly lifelike video game.

But in the new order of meaning, Baudrillard’s one, this relationship has been inverted, and representations give meaning to the world. This doesn’t just mean that life sometimes imitates art. It means that all representations, including video games, advertisements, movies, TikTok videos, you name it, work together to create a universe of symbols that feel realer to us than reality. And that in fact subsume reality altogether.

Baudrillard argued that the characteristic mental disorder of this new arrangement was schizophrenia. Because he was a French theorist, he was being edgy and didn’t mean the actual disease. He meant a state of terrified confusion, brought on by the relentless bombardment of contextless signs. Humans no longer have an autonomous inner self that can point our attention at this or that; we are powerless nodes, receiving and transmitting superficial fragments of media that stimulate our emotions and bypass our understanding.

Baudrillard wrote all this in the 1980s, roughly 20 years before the invention of the iPhone, and it describes exactly how we experience reality today — about 20 years since its release. And as a result, there is no single media product that can compete with the world of fleeting and insane impressions that is always a glance away. Certainly, G.T.A. VI can’t. It will be absorbed into the greater world of fragments and sensations through which most of us now experience culture. There it will be regurgitated in often-garbled forms, sometimes by nonpeople, according to rules written by nonpeople, for a human audience addicted to garbled regurgitation. In another 13 years it will be 2039. You don’t have to work for Anthropic to know that the way humans represent and understand their lives is probably going to look different.

This is the paradox of Rockstar’s grand undertaking: It has crafted a working miniature of the United States during a period in which the American sense of reality has almost completely broken down; a period in which the desire for grand attempts at sense-making have been subordinated to the desire for distraction; a period in which American disorder has moved from the outside world to our innermost selves. It is a coherent map of incoherent territory — maybe the last one.
